torpescent.c: Torpescent Tor*pes"cent (?), a. [L. torpescens, p. pr. of torpescere to grow stiff, numb, or torpid, incho. fr. torpere. See Torpid.] Becoming torpid or numb. Shenstone.

torpid.c: Torpid Tor"pid (tôr"pĭd), a. [L. torpidus, fr. torpere to be stiff, numb, or torpid; of uncertain origin.] 1. Having lost motion, or the power of exertion and feeling; numb; benumbed; as, a torpid limb.
Torpid Tor"pid (?), n. [See Torpid, a.] [Slang, Oxford University, Eng.] 1. An inferior racing boat, or one who rows in such a boat.

torpidly.c: Torpidly Tor"pid*ly (?), adv. In a torpid manner.

torpidness.c: Torpidness Tor"pid*ness, n. The qualityy or state of being torpid.

torpify.c: Torpify Tor"pi*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Torpified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Torpifying. (?).] [L. torpere to be torpid + -fy.] To make torpid; to numb, or benumb.

torpitude.c: Torpitude Tor"pi*tude (?), n. Torpidness. [Obs.] “In a kind of torpitude, or sleeping state.” Derham.

torpor.c: Torpor Tor"por (?), n. [L., from torpere, to be torpid.]

torporific.c: Torporific Tor`por*if"ic (?), a. [L. torpor torpor + facere to make.] Tending to produce torpor.

torquate.c: Torquate Tor"quate (?), a. [L. torquatus wearing a collar.] (Zool.) Collared; having a torques, or distinct colored ring around the neck.

torquated.c: torquated tor"qua*ted (?), a. [L. Torqyatus.] Having or wearing a torque, or neck chain.

torque.c: Torque Torque (?), n. [L. torques a twisted neck chain, fr. torquere to twist.] 1. A collar or neck chain, usually twisted, especially as worn by ancient barbaric nations, as the Gauls, Germans, and Britons.

torqued.c: Torqued Torqued (?), a. [L. torquere to twist, to turn, to wind.] 1. Wreathed; twisted. [R.]

torques.c: Torques ‖Tor"ques (?), n. [L., a necklace. See Torque, 1.] (Zool.) A cervical ring of hair or feathers, distinguished by its color or structure; a collar.

torrefaction.c: Torrefaction Tor`re*fac"tion (?), n. [L. torrefacere,torrefactum, to torrefy: cf. F. torréfaction. See Torrefy.] The act or process of torrefying, or the state of being torrefied. Bp. Hall.

torrefy.c: Torrefy Tor"re*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Torrefied (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Torrefying.] [L. torrere to parch + -fy: cf. F. torréfier, L. torrefacere.] [Written also torrify.] 1. To dry by a fire. Sir T. Browne.

torrens.c: Torrens system Tor"rens sys`tem (?). A system of registration of titles to land (as distinct from registration of deeds) introduced into South Australia by the Real Property (or Torrens) Act (act 15 of 1857-58), drafted by Sir Robert Torrens (1814-84). Its essential feature is the guaranty by the government of properly registered titles. The system has been generally adopted in Australia and British Columbia, and in its original or a modified form in some other countries, including some States of the United States. Hence Torrens title, etc.

torrent.c: Torrent Tor"rent (?), n. [F., fr. L. torrens, -entis, fr. torrens burning, roaring, boiling, p. pr. of torrere to dry by heat, to burn. See Torrid.] 1. A violent stream, as of water, lava, or the like; a stream suddenly raised and running rapidly, as down a precipice.
Torrent Tor"rent, a. [See Torrent, n.] Rolling or rushing in a rapid stream. “Waves of torrent fire.” Milton.

torrentine.c: Torrentine Torrential { Tor*ren"tial (?), Tor*ren"tine (?), } a. Of or pertaining to a torrent; having the character of a torrent; caused by a torrent. [R.]

torricellian.c: Torricellian Tor`ri*cel"li*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Torricelli, an Italian philosopher and mathematician, who, in 1643, discovered that the rise of a liquid in a tube, as in the barometer, is due to atmospheric pressure. See Barometer.

torrid.c: Torrid Tor"rid (?), a. [L. torridus, fr. torrere to parch, to burn, akin to E. Thist: cf. F. torride. See Thirst.] 1. Parched; dried with heat; as, a torrid plain or desert. “Barca or Cyrene's torrid soil.” Milton.

torridness.c: Torridness Tor"rid*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being torrid or parched.

torril.c: Torril Tor"ril (?), n. A worthless woman; also, a worthless horse. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

torsade.c: Torsade Tor*sade" (?), n. [F.] A twisted cord; also, a molded or worked ornament of similar form.

torse.c: Torse Torse (?), n. [OF., fr. OF. & F. tors, torse, twisted, wreathed, p. p. of tordre to twist, L. torquere. See Torture.]

torsel.c: Torsel Tor"sel (?), n. (Carp.) A plate of timber for the end of a beam or joist to rest on. Gwilt

torsibillty.c: Torsibillty Tor`si*bil"l*ty (?), n. The tendency, as of a rope, to untwist after being twisted.

torsion.c: Torsion Tor"sion (?), n. [F., fr. LL. torsio, fr. L. torquere, tortum, to twist. See Torture.] 1. The act of turning or twisting, or the state of being twisted; the twisting or wrenching of a body by the exertion of a lateral force tending to turn one end or part of it about a longitudinal axis, while the other is held fast or turned in the opposite direction.
Torsion electrometer Tor"sion e*lec*trom"e*ter. (Elec.) A torsion balance used for measuring electric attraction or repulsion.
Torsion galvanometer Torsion galvanometer. (Elec.) A galvanometer in which current is measured by torsion.
Torsion head Torsion head. That part of a torsion balance from which the wire or filament is suspended.
Torsion indicator Torsion indicator. An autographic torsion meter.

Torsion meter Torsion meter. (Mech.) An instrument for determining the torque on a shaft, and hence the horse power of an engine, esp. of a marine engine of high power, by measuring the amount of twist of a given length of the shaft. Called also torsimeter, torsiometer, torsometer.

torsional.c: Torsional Tor"sion*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to torsion; resulting from torsion, or the force with which a thread or wire returns to a state of rest after having been twisted round its axis; as, torsional force.

torsk.c: Torsk Torsk (?), n. [Dan.; akin to Icel. þorskr a codfish, G. dorsch.] (Zool.) (a) The cusk. See Cusk. (b) The codfish. Called also tusk.

torso.c: Torso Tor"so (?), n.; pl. E. Torsos (#), It. Torsi (#). [It. torso, probably fr. L. thyrsus a stalk, stem, thyrsus, Gr.?; cf. OHG. torso, turso, a stalk, stem, G. dorsche a cabbage stalk. Cf. Thyrsus, Truss.] The human body, as distinguished from the head and limbs; in sculpture, the trunk of a statue, mutilated of head and limbs; as, the torso of Hercules.

tort.c: Tort Tort (?), n. [F., from LL. tortum, fr. L. tortus twisted, crooked, p. p. of torqure to twist, bend. See Torture.] 1. Mischief; injury; calamity. [Obs.]

torta.c: Torta Tor"ta (?), n. [Cf. Sp. torta a cake.] (Metal.) a flat heap of moist, crushed silver ore, prepared for the patio process.

torteau.c: Torteau Tor"teau (?), n.; pl. Torteaus (#). [Of. torteau, tortel, from L. tortus twisted. See Tort.] (Her.) A roundel of a red color.

torticollis.c: Torticollis Tor`ti*col"lis (?), n. [F. toricolis; L. torquere, tortum, to twist + collum the neck.] (Med.) See Wryneck.

tortile.c: Tortile Tor"tile (?), a. [L. tortilis, fr. torquere, tortum, to twist: cf. F. tortile.] Twisted; wreathed; coiled.

tortility.c: Tortility Tor*til"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being tortile, twisted, or wreathed.

tortilla.c: Tortilla ‖Tor*til"la (?), n. [Sp.] An unleavened cake, as of maize flour, baked on a heated iron or stone.

tortion.c: Tortion Tor"tion (?), n. [LL. tortio. See Torsion.] Torment; pain. [Obs.] Bacon.

tortious.c: Tortious Tor"tious (?), a. [From Tort.] 1. Injurious; wrongful. [Obs.] “Tortious power.” Spenser.

tortiously.c: Tortiously Tor"tious*ly, adv. (Law) In a tortous manner.

tortive.c: Tortive Tor"tive (?), a. [L. tortus, p. p. of torquere to twist, wind.] Twisted; wreathed. Shak.

tortoise.c: Tortoise Tor"toise (?), n. [OE. tortuce, fr. OF. tortis crooked, fr. L. tortus twisted, crooked, contorted, p. p. of torquere, tortum, to wind; cf. F. tortue tortoise, LL. tortuca, tartuca, Pr. tortesa crookedness, tortis crooked. so called in allusion to its crooked feet. See Torture.] 1. (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of reptiles of the order Testudinata.

tortoiseshell.c: tortoise-shell tortoise-shell, adj. Having a color like that of a tortoise's shell, black with white and orange spots; -- used mostly to describe cats of that color. n. a tortoise-shell cat.

tortricid.c: Tortricid Tor"tri*cid (?), a. [See Tortrix.] (Zool.) Of or pertaining to Tortix, or the family Tortricidae.

tortrix.c: Tortrix ‖Tor"trix (?), n. [NL., fr. L. torquere, tortum, to twist.] 1. (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of small moths of the family Tortricidae, the larvae of which usually roll up the leaves of plants on which they live; -- also called leaf roller.

tortulous.c: Tortulous Tor"tu*lous (tôr"tu*lŭs; 135), a. (Nat. Hist.) Swelled out at intervals like a knotted cord.

tortuose.c: Tortuose Tor"tu*ose` (?), a. [See Tortuous.] Wreathed; twisted; winding. Loudon

tortuoslty.c: Tortuoslty Tor`tu*os"l*ty (?), n. [L. tortuositas: cf. F. tortuosite.] the quality or state of being tortuous.

tortuous.c: Tortuous Tor"tu*ous (?), a. [OE. tortuos, L. tortuosus, fr. tortus a twisting, winding, fr. torquere, tortum, to twist: cf. F. tortueux. See Torture.] 1. Bent in different directions; wreathed; twisted; winding; as, a tortuous train; a tortuous leaf or corolla.

torturable.c: Torturable Tor"tur*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being tortured.

torture.c: Torture Tor"ture (tôr"tur; 135), n. [F., fr. L. tortura, fr. torquere, tortum, to twist, rack, torture; probably akin to Gr. tre`pein to turn, G. drechseln to turn on a lathe, and perhaps to E. queer. Cf. Contort, Distort, Extort, Retort, Tart, n., Torch, Torment, Tortion, Tort, Trope.] 1. Extreme pain; anguish of body or mind; pang; agony; torment; as, torture of mind. Shak.
torture tor"ture, v. t. [imp. & p. p. tortured (tôr"turd; 135); p. pr. & vb. n. tTorturing.] [Cf. F. Torturer. ] 1. To put to torture; to pain extremely; to harass; to vex.

torturer.c: Torturer Tor"tur*er (tôr"tur*ẽr), n. One who tortures; a tormentor.

torturingly.c: Torturingly Tor"tur*ing*ly, adv. So as to torture. Beau. & Fl.

torturous.c: Torturous Tor"tur*ous (tôr"tur*ŭs), a. Involving, or pertaining to, torture. [R.] “The torturous crucifixion.” I. Disraeli.

torula.c: Torula ‖Tor"u*la (?), n.; pl. Torulae (?) [NL., dim. of L. torus a semicircular molding.] (Biol.) (a) A chain of special bacteria. (b) A genus of budding fungi. Same as Saccharomyces. Also used adjectively.

torulaform.c: Torulaform Tor"u*la*form` (?), a. (Biol.) Having the appearance of a torula; in the form of a little chain; as, a torulaform string of micrococci.

torulose.c: Torulose Tor"u*lose (?), a. [L. torulus, dim. of torus: cf. F. toruleux. See Torus] (Bot.) Same as Torose.

torus.c: Torus ‖To"rus (tō"rŭs), n.; pl. Tori (tō"rī). [L., a round, swelling, or bulging place, an elevation. Cf. 3d Tore.]

torved.c: Torved Torved (?), a. Stern; grim. See Torvous. [Obs.]

torvity.c: Torvity Tor"vi*ty (?), a. [L. torvitas. See Torvous.] Sourness or severity of countenance; sternness. [Obs.]

torvous.c: Torvous Tor"vous (?), a. [L. torvus. ] Sour of aspect; of a severe countenance; stern; grim. [Obs.]

tory.c: Tory To"ry (?), n.; pl. Tories (#). [ Properly used of the Irish bogtrotters who robbed and plundered during the English civil wars, professing to be in sympathy with the royal cause; hence transferred to those who sought to maintain the extreme prerogatives of the crown; probably from Ir. toiridhe, tor, a pursuer; akin to Ir. & Gael. toir a pursuit.] 1. (Eng. Politics) A member of the conservative party, as opposed to the progressive party which was formerly called the Whig, and is now called the Liberal, party; an earnest supporter of existing royal and ecclesiastical authority.
Tory To"ry (?), a. Of or pertaining to the Tories.

toryism.c: Toryism To"ry*ism (?), n. The principles of the Tories.

toscatter.c: Toscatter To*scat"ter (?), v. t. [Pref. to- + scatter.] To scatter in pieces; to divide. [Obs.] Chaucer.

tose.c: Tose Tose (?), v. t. [ See Touse ] To tease, or comb, as wool. [Obs.or Prov. Eng.]

tosh.c: Tosh Tosh (?), a. [Cf. OF. tonce shorn, clipped, and E. tonsure.] Neat; trim. [Scot.] Jomieson.

toshred.c: Toshred To*shred" (?), v. t. [Pref. to- + shred. ] To cut into shreds or pieces. [Obs.] Chaucer.

toss.c: Toss Toss (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Tossed (?); (less properly Tost); p. pr. & vb. n. Tossing.] [ W. tosiaw, tosio, to jerk, toss, snatch, tosa quick jerk, a toss, a snatch. ] 1. To throw with the hand; especially, to throw with the palm of the hand upward, or to throw upward; as, to toss a ball.
Toss Toss, v. i. 1. To roll and tumble; to be in violent commotion; to write; to fling.
Toss Toss, n. 1. A throwing upward, or with a jerk; the act of tossing; as, the toss of a ball.

tosser.c: Tosser Toss"er (?), n. One who tosses. J. Fletcher.

tossily.c: Tossily Toss"i*ly (?), adv. In a tossy manner. [R.]

tossing.c: Tossing Toss"ing, n. 1. The act of throwing upward; a rising and falling suddenly; a rolling and tumbling.

tosspot.c: Tosspot Toss"pot` (?), n. A toper; one habitually given to strong drink; a drunkard. Shak.

tossy.c: Tossy Toss"y (?), a. Tossing the head, as in scorn or pride; hence, proud; contemptuous; scornful; affectedly indifferent; as, a tossy commonplace. [R.] C. Kingsley.

tost.c: Tost Tost (?), imp. & p. p. of Toss.

toswink.c: Toswink To*swink" (?), v. i. [Pref. to- + swink.] To labor excessively. [Obs.] Chaucer.

tot.c: Tot Tot (?), n. [Cf. Toddle, Tottle, Totter.] 1. Anything small; -- frequently applied as a term of endearment to a little child.
Tot Tot (?), n. [L.] Lit., so much; -- a term used in the English exchequer to indicate that a debt was good or collectible for the amount specified, and often written opposite the item.
Tot Tot, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Totted; p. pr. & vb. n. Totting.] 1. To mark with the word “tot”; as, a totted debt. See Tot, n.

tota.c: Tota To"ta (?), n. [From the native name in Egypt.] (Zool.) The grivet.

total.c: Total To"tal (?), a. [F., fr. LL. totalis, fr. L. tolus all,whole. Cf. Factotum, Surtout, Teetotum.] Whole; not divided; entire; full; complete; absolute; as, a total departure from the evidence; a total loss. “ Total darkness.” “To undergo myself the total crime.” Milton.
Total To"tal, n. The whole; the whole sum or amount; as, these sums added make the grand total of five millions.
Total To"tal (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Totaled (?) or Totalled; p. pr. & vb. n. Totaling or Totalling.] 1. To bring to a total; also, to reach as a total; to amount to. [Colloq.]

totalis.c: Totalis To"tal*is (?), n. [See Total, a.] The total.

totality.c: Totality To*tal"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. totalite, LL. totalitas.] 1. The quality or state of being total; as, the totality of an eclipse.

totalization.c: Totalization To`tal*i*za"tion (?), n. Act of totalizing, or state of being totalized.

totalizator.c: Totalizator To"tal*i*za`tor (?), n. [From Totalize: cf. F. totalisateur.] A machine for registering and indicating the number and nature of bets made on horse races. Called also totalizer.

totalize.c: Totalize To"tal*ize (?), v. t. To make total, or complete; to reduce to completeness. Coleridge.
Totalize To"tal*ize, v. i. To use a totalizator.

totally.c: Totally To"tal*ly, adv. In a total manner; wholly; entirely.

totalness.c: Totalness To"tal*ness, n. The quality or state of being total; entireness; totality.

totara.c: Totara To"ta*ra (?), n. [Maori.] A coniferous tree (Podocarpus totara), next to the kauri the most valuable timber tree of New Zealand. Its hard reddish wood is used for furniture and building, esp. in wharves, bridges, etc. Also mahogany pine.

tote.c: Tote Tote (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Toted; p. pr. & vb. n. Toting.] [Said to be of African origin.] To carry or bear; as, to tote a child over a stream; to tote a gun on one's hip; -- a colloquial word originating in the Southern States, and used there esp. by negroes, now common throughout the U. S.
Tote Tote, n. [L. totum, fr. totus all, whole.] The entire body, or all; as, the whole tote. [Colloq.]

totear.c: Totear To*tear" (?), v. t. [Pref. to- + tear. ] To tear or rend in pieces. [Obs.] Chaucer.

totem.c: Totem To"tem (?), n. [Massachusetts Indian wutohtimoin that to which a person or place belongs.] 1. A rude picture, as of a bird, beast, or the like, used by the North American Indians as a symbolic designation, as of a family or a clan; also, the object or animal itself, considered as an symbol of the family.

Totem post Totem pole { To"tem pole or To"tem post }. A pole or pillar, carved and painted with a series of totemic symbols, set up before the house of certain Indian tribes of the northwest coast of North America, esp. Indians of the Koluschan stock.

totemic.c: Totemic To*tem"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to a totem, or totemism.

totemism.c: Totemism To"tem*ism (?), n. 1. The system of distinguishing families, clans, etc., in a tribe by the totem.

totemist.c: Totemist To"tem*ist, n. One belonging to a clan or tribe having a totem. -- To`tem*is"tic (#), a.

toter.c: Toter Tot"er (?), n. [See Tote to carry.] (Zool.) The stone roller. See Stone roller (a), under Stone.

tother.c: T'other T'oth"er (?). A colloquial contraction of the other, and formerly a contraction for that other. See the Note under That, 2.

totipalmate.c: Totipalmate To`ti*pal"mate (?), a. [L. totus all, whole + E. palmate.] (Zool.) Having all four toes united by a web; -- said of certain sea birds, as the pelican and the gannet. See Illust. under Aves.

totipalmi.c: Totipalmi ‖To`ti*pal"mi (?), n. pl. [NL., from L. totus all, whole + palmus palm.] (Zool.) A division of swimming birds including those that have totipalmate feet.

totipresence.c: Totipresence To`ti*pres"ence (?), n. [L. totus all, whole + E. presence.] Omnipresence. [Obs.] A. Tucker.

totipresent.c: Totipresent To`ti*pres"ent (?), a. [L. totus all, whole + E. present.] Omnipresent. [Obs.] A. Tucker.

totter.c: Totter Tot"ter (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Tottered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Tottering.] [Probably for older tolter; cf. AS. tealtrian to totter, vacillate. Cf.Tilt to incline, Toddle, Tottle, Totty.] 1. To shake so as to threaten a fall; to vacillate; to be unsteady; to stagger; as, an old man totters with age. “As a bowing wall shall ye be, and as a tottering fence.” Ps. lxii. 3.

totteringly.c: Totteringly Tot"ter*ing*ly, adv. In a tottering manner.

tottery.c: Tottery Tot"ter*y (?), a. Trembling or vaccilating, as if about to fall; unsteady; shaking. Johnson.

tottle.c: Tottle Tot"tle (tŏt"t'l), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Tottled (tŏt"t'ld); p. pr. & vb. n. Tottling (tŏt"tlĭng).] [See Toddle, Totter.] To walk in a wavering, unsteady manner; to toddle; to topple. [Colloq.]

tottlish.c: Tottlish Tot"tlish (tŏt"tlĭsh), a. Trembling or tottering, as if about to fall; unsteady. [Colloq. U. S.]

totty.c: Totty Tot"ty (?), a. [OE. toti. Cf. Totter.] Unsteady; dizzy; tottery. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Sir W. Scott.

toty.c: Toty To"ty (?), n. A sailor or fisherman; -- so called in some parts of the Pacific.

toucan.c: Toucan Tou"can (tōo"kăn; 277), n. [F., fr. Pg. tucano; from Brazilian name. ] 1. (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of fruit-eating birds of tropical America belonging to Ramphastos, Pteroglossus, and allied genera of the family Ramphastidae. They have a very large, but light and thin, beak, often nearly as long as the body itself. Most of the species are brilliantly colored with red, yellow, white, and black in striking contrast.

touch.c: Touch Touch (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Touched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Touching.] [F. toucher, OF. touchier, tuchier; of Teutonic origin; cf. OHG. zucchen, zukken, to twitch, pluck, draw, G. zukken, zukken, v. intens. fr. OHG. ziohan to draw, G. ziehen, akin to E. tug. See Tuck, v. t., Tug, and cf. Tocsin, Toccata.] 1. To come in contact with; to hit or strike lightly against; to extend the hand, foot, or the like, so as to reach or rest on.
Touch Touch (?), v. i. 1. To be in contact; to be in a state of junction, so that no space is between; as, two spheres touch only at points. Johnson.
Touch Touch, n. [Cf. F. touche. See Touch, v. ] 1. The act of touching, or the state of being touched; contact.

touchable.c: Touchable Touch"a*ble (tŭch"ȧ*b'l), a. Capable of being touched; tangible. -- Touch"a*ble*ness, n.

touchback.c: Touchback Touch"back` (tŭch"băk`), n. (Football) The act of touching the football down by a player behind his own goal line when it received its last impulse from an opponent; -- distinguished from safety touchdown.

touchbox.c: Touch-box Touch"-box` (tŭch"bŏks`), n. A box containing lighted tinder, formerly carried by soldiers who used matchlocks, to kindle the match.

touchdown.c: Touchdown Touch"down` (tŭch"doun`), n. (Football) The act of touching the football down behind the opponents' goal; also the score (6 points) resulting from such a play.

touchhole.c: Touchhole Touch"hole` (tŭch"hōl`), n. The vent of a cannon or other firearm, by which fire is communicateed to the powder of the charge.

touchily.c: Touchily Touch"i*ly (tŭch"ĭ*ly̆), adv. In a touchy manner.

touchiness.c: Touchiness Touch"i*ness (tŭch"ĭ*nĕs), n. The quality or state of being touchy; peevishness; irritability; irascibility.

touching.c: Touching Touch"ing (tŭch"ĭng), a. Affecting; moving; pathetic; as, a touching tale. -- Touch"ing*ly (#), adv.
Touching Touch"ing, prep. Concerning; with respect to.
Touching Touch"ing, n. The sense or act of feeling; touch.

touchmenot.c: Touch-me-not Touch"-me-not` (tŭch"me*nŏt`), n. (Bot.) (a) See Impatiens. (b) Squirting cucumber. See under Cucumber.

touchneedle.c: Touch-needle Touch"-nee`dle (?), n. (Metal.) A small bar of gold and silver, either pure, or alloyed in some known proportion with copper, for trying the purity of articles of gold or silver by comparison of the streaks made by the article and the bar on a touchstone.

touchpaper.c: Touch-paper Touch"-pa`per (?), n. Paper steeped in saltpeter, which burns slowly, and is used as a match for firing gunpowder, and the like.

touchstone.c: Touchstone Touch"stone` (?), n. 1. (Min.) Lydian stone; basanite; -- so called because used to test the purity of gold and silver by the streak which is left upon the stone when it is rubbed by the metal. See Basanite.

touchwood.c: Touchwood Touch"wood` (?), n. [Probably for tachwood; OE. tache tinder (of uncertain origin) + wood.]

touchy.c: Touchy Touch"y (?), a. [For techy, tetchy.] Peevish; irritable; irascible; techy; apt to take fire. [Colloq.]

tough.c: Tough Tough (?), a. [Compar. Tougher (?); superl. Toughest.] [OE. tough, AS. tōh, akin to D. taai, LG. taa, tage, tau, OHG. zāhi, G. zähe, and also to AS. getenge near to, close to, oppressive, OS. bitengi.] 1. Having the quality of flexibility without brittleness; yielding to force without breaking; capable of resisting great strain; as, the ligaments of animals are remarkably tough. “Tough roots and stubs. ” Milton.

toughen.c: Toughen Tough"en (?), v. i. & t. [imp. & p. p. Toughened (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Toughening.] To grow or make tough, or tougher.

toughhead.c: Tough-head Tough"-head` (?), n. (Zool.) The ruddy duck. [ Local U. S. ]

toughish.c: Toughish Tough"ish, a. Tough in a slight degree.

toughly.c: Toughly Tough"ly, adv. In a tough manner.

toughness.c: Toughness Tough"ness, n. The quality or state of being tough.

toughpitch.c: Tough-pitch Tough"-pitch` (?), n. (Metal.) (a) The exact state or quality of texture and consistency of well reduced and refined copper. (b) Copper so reduced; -- called also tough-cake.

touite.c: Touite Tou"ite (?), n. The wood warbler. [Prov. Eng.]

toupet.c: Toupet Toupee { Tou*pee" (?; 277), Tou*pet" (?; 277) } (?), n. [F. toupet, dim. of OF. top a tuft; of Teutonic origin, and akin to E. top. See Top apex, and cf. Topet.]

toupettit.c: Toupettit Tou"pet*tit (?), n. [See Topet, toupee.] (Zool.) The crested titmouse. [Prov. Eng.]

tour.c: Tour Tour (?), n. [F. tour. See Tower.] A tower. [Obs.] Chaucer.

Tour Tour (?), n. [F. tour. See Turn, v. t.] 1. A going round; a circuit; hence, a journey in a circuit; a prolonged circuitous journey; a comprehensive excursion; as, the tour of Europe; the tour of France or England.
Tour Tour (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Toured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Touring.] To make a tourm; as, to tour throught a country. T. Hughes.

tourbillion.c: Tourbillion Tour*bil"lion (?), n. [F. torbillion a whirlwind, tourbillion, fr. L. turbo, -inis, a whirl, whirlwind.] An ornamental firework which turns round, when in the air, so as to form a scroll of fire. G. Francis.

touring.c: Touring car Tour"ing car. An automobile designed for touring; specif., a roomy car, not a limousine, for five or more passengers.

tourist.c: Tourist Tour"ist (?), n. One who makes a tour, or performs a journey, especially for pleasure.

tourmaline.c: Tourmaline Tour"ma*line (?), n. [F. tourmaline, cf. It. turmalina, tormalina, NL. turmalina, turmalinus; all fr. tournamal, a name given to this stone in Ceylon.] (Min.) A mineral occurring usually in three-sided or six-sided prisms terminated by rhombohedral or scalenohedral planes. Black tourmaline (schorl) is the most common variety, but there are also other varieties, as the blue (indicolite), red (rubellite), also green, brown, and white. The red and green varieties when transparent are valued as jewels. [Written also turmaline.]

tourn.c: Tourn Tourn (?), n. [See Turn] 1. A spinning wheel. [Prov. Eng.]

tournament.c: Tournament Tour"na*ment (?), n. [OE. turnement, tornement, OF. torneiement, tornoiement, F. tournoiement a turning or wheeling round. See Tourney.] 1. A mock fight, or warlike game, formerly in great favor, in which a number of combatants were engaged, as an exhibition of their address and bravery; hence, figuratively, a real battle. “In battle and in tourneyment.” Chaucer.

tournery.c: Tournery Tourn"er*y (?), n. Work turned on a lathe; turnery. [Obs.] See Turnery. Evelyn.

tourney.c: Tourney Tour"ney (?), n. [OF. tornei, tornoi, F. tournoi, fr. OF. torneier, tornoier, tournoier, to tit, to tourney, F. tournoyer to turn round and round. See Turn, v. t.] A tournament. Bacon.
Tourney Tour"ney, v. i. [Cf.OF. torneier. See Tourney, n. ] To perform in tournaments; to tilt.

tourniquet.c: Tourniquet Tour"ni*quet (?), n. [F., fr. tourner to turn.] (Surg.) An instrument for arresting hemorrhage. It consists essentially of a pad or compress upon which pressure is made by a band which is tightened by a screw or other means.

tournois.c: Tournois ‖Tour`nois" (?), n. [F., belonging to Tours in France.] A former French money of account worth 20 sous, or a franc. It was thus called in distinction from the Paris livre, which contained 25 sous.

touze.c: Touze Touse { Touse, Touze (touz) }, v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Toused (touzd); p. pr. & vb. n. Tousing.] [OE. tosen. √64. See tease, and cf. Tose, Toze.] To pull; to haul; to tear; to worry. [Prov. Eng.] Shak.
Touze Touze (touz), v. t. & i. See Touse. [Prov. Eng.]

touse.c: Touse Touse (touz), n. A pulling; a disturbance. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

tousel.c: Tousel Tous"el (?), v. t. Same as Tousle. [Colloq.]

touser.c: Touser Tous"er (?), n. One who touses. [Prov. Eng.]

tousle.c: Tousle Tou"sle (?), v. t. [Freq. of touse. Cf.Tossle.] To put into disorder; to tumble; to touse. [Colloq.]

touslesmois.c: Tous-les-mois Tous`-les`-mois" (?), n. [F., all the months, i. e., every month.] A kind of starch with very large, oval, flattened grains, often sold as arrowroot, and extensively used for adulterating cocoa. It is made from the rootstocks of a species of Canna, probably Canna edulis, the tubers of which are edible every month in the year.

tousy.c: Tousy Tou"sy (?), a. [See Touse, n. & v.] Tousled; tangled; rough; shaggy. [Colloq.]

tout.c: Tout Tout (tōot), v. i. [See 1st Toot.] 1. To act as a tout. See 2d Tout. [Cant. Eng.]
Tout Tout (tout; tōot; Scot. & dial. tōot), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Touted; p. pr. & vb. n. Touting.] 1. To look narrowly; spy. [Scot. & Dial. Eng.]
Tout Tout, n. One who secretly watches race horses which are in course of training, to get information about their capabilities, for use in betting. [Cant. Eng.]
Tout Tout (tōot), n. [Prob. fr. F. tout all.] In the game of solo, a proposal to win all eight tricks.
Tout Tout, v. i. [See 3d Toot. ] To toot a horn.

Tout Tout, v. t. (Horse Racing) (a) To spy out information about, as a racing stable or horse. [Cant, Eng.] (b) To give a tip on (a race horse) to a better with the expectation of sharing in the latter's winnings. [Cant, U. S.]

toutensemble.c: Tout-ensemble ‖Tout`-en`sem"ble (?), n. [F.] All together; hence, in costume, the fine arts, etc., the general effect of a work as a whole, without regard to the execution of the separate perts.

touter.c: Touter Tout"er (?), n. One who seeks customers, as for an inn, a public conveyance, shops, and the like: hence, an obtrusive candidate for office. [Colloq.]

tow.c: Tow Tow (tō), n. [OE. tow, AS. tow, akin to OD. touw, Icel. tō a tuft of wool for spinning; cf. E. taw, v. t.] The coarse and broken part of flax or hemp, separated from the finer part by the hatchel or swingle.

Tow Tow, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Towed (tōd); p. pr. & vb. n. Towing.] [OE. towen, toȝen; akin to OFries. toga to pull about, OHG. zogōn, Icel. toga, AS. tohline a towline, and AS. teón to draw, p. p. getogen. See Tug.] To draw or pull through the water, as a vessel of any kind, by means of a rope.
Tow Tow (?), n. [Cf. Icel. taug a rope, from the same root as E. tow, v. t.] 1. A rope by which anything is towed; a towline, or towrope.

towage.c: Towage Tow"age (?), n. [From Tow, v..cf. F. touage.] 1. The act of towing.

towards.c: Towards Toward { To"ward, To"wards } (?), prep.[AS.? impending, imminent, future, toward,? towards. See To, and -ward, wards.] 1. In the direction of; to.
Towards Toward { To"ward, To"wards } adv. Near; at hand; in state of preparation.

toward.c: Toward To"ward (?), a. [AS.?. See Toward, prep.] 1. Approaching; coming near. “His toward peril.” Spenser.

towardliness.c: Towardliness To"ward*li*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being towardly; docility; tractableness.

towardly.c: Towardly To"ward*ly, a. Same as Toward, a., 2.

towardness.c: Towardness To"ward*ness, n. Quality or state of being toward.

towboat.c: Towboat Tow"boat` (?), n. 1. A vessel constructed for being towed, as a canal boat.

towel.c: Towel Tow"el (?), n. [OE. towaille, towail, F. touaille, LL. toacula, of Teutonic origin; cf. OHG. dwahila, swahilla, G. zwehle, fr. OHG. dwahan to wash; akin to D. dwaal a towel, AS. þweán to wash, OS. thwahan, Icel. þvā, Sw. två, Dan. toe, Goth. þwahan. Cf. Doily.] A cloth used for wiping, especially one used for drying anything wet, as the person after a bath.
Towel Tow"el, v. t. To beat with a stick. [Prov. Eng.]

toweling.c: Toweling Tow"el*ing, n. Cloth for towels, especially such as is woven in long pieces to be cut at will, as distinguished from that woven in towel lengths with borders, etc. [Written also towelling.]

tower.c: Tower Tow"er (?), n. [OE. tour,tor,tur, F. tour, L. turris; akin to Gr.?; cf. W. twr a tower, Ir. tor a castle, Gael. torr a tower, castle. Cf. Tor, Turret.] 1. (Arch.) (a) A mass of building standing alone and insulated, usually higher than its diameter, but when of great size not always of that proportion. (b) A projection from a line of wall, as a fortification, for purposes of defense, as a flanker, either or the same height as the curtain wall or higher. (c) A structure appended to a larger edifice for a special purpose, as for a belfry, and then usually high in proportion to its width and to the height of the rest of the edifice; as, a church tower.
Tower Tow"er (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. towered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. towering.] To rise and overtop other objects; to be lofty or very high; hence, to soar.
Tower Tow"er, v. t. To soar into. [Obs.] Milton.

towered.c: Towered Tow"ered (?), a. Adorned or defended by towers.

towering.c: Towering Tow"er*ing (?), a. 1. Very high; elevated; rising aloft; as, a towering height. Pope.

towery.c: Towery Tow"er*y (?), a. Having towers; adorned or defended by towers. [R.] “Towery cities.” Pope.

towhead.c: Tow-head Tow"-head` (?), n. 1. An urchin who has soft, whitish hair. [Colloq.]

towilly.c: Towilly To*wil"ly (?), n. (Zool.) The sanderling; -- so called from its cry. [Prov. Eng.]

towline.c: Towline Tow"line` (?), n. [AS. tohline. See Tow, v. t., and Line. ] (Naut.) A line used to tow vessels; a towrope.

town.c: Town Town (toun), n. [OE. toun, tun, AS. tun inclosure, fence, village, town; akin to D. tuin a garden, G. zaun a hadge, fence, OHG. zun, Icel. tun an inclosure, homestead, house, Ir. & Gael. dun a fortress, W. din. Cf. Down, adv. & prep., Dune, tine to inclose.] 1. Formerly: (a) An inclosure which surrounded the mere homestead or dwelling of the lord of the manor. [Obs.] (b) The whole of the land which constituted the domain. [Obs.] (c) A collection of houses inclosed by fences or walls. [Obs.] Palsgrave.

towncrier.c: Town-crier Town"-cri`er (?), n. A town officer who makes proclamations to the people; the public crier of a town.

towned.c: Towned Towned (?), a. Having towns; containing many towns. [Obs.] Hakluyt.

townhall.c: Townhall Town"hall` (?), n. A public hall or building, belonging to a town, where the public offices are established, the town council meets, the people assemble in town meeting, etc.

townhouse.c: Townhouse Town"house` (?), n. A building devoted to the public used of a town; a townhall.

townish.c: Townish Town"ish, a. Of or pertaining to the inhabitants of a town; like the town. [R.] Turbervile.

townless.c: Townless Town"less, a. Having no town. Howell.

townlet.c: Townlet Town"let (?), n. A small town. North Brit. Rev.

townsfolk.c: Townsfolk Towns"folk` (?), n. The people of a town; especially, the inhabitants of a city, in distinction from country people; townspeople.

township.c: Township Town"ship (?), n. 1. The district or territory of a town.

townspeople.c: Townspeople Towns"peo`ple (?), n. The inhabitants of a town or city, especially in distinction from country people; townsfolk.

townwards.c: Townwards Townward { Town"ward, Town"wards (?), } (?), adv. Toward a town. Longfellow.

towpath.c: Towpath Tow"path` (?), n. A path traveled by men or animals in towing boats; -- called also towing path.

towrope.c: Towrope Tow"rope` (?), n. A rope used in towing vessels.

towser.c: Towser Tow"ser (tou"zẽr), n. [See Touse to pull about. ] A familiar name for a dog. [ Written also Towzer. ]

towy.c: Towy Tow"y (tō"y̆), a. Composed of, or like, tow.

toxaemia.c: Toxaemia ‖Tox*æ"mi*a (tŏks"ē"mĭ*ȧ), a. [NL., fr. Gr. toxiko`n poison + a"i^ma blood.] (Med.) Blood poisoning. See under Blood.

toxalbumin.c: Toxalbumin Tox`al*bu"min (?), n. [See Toxic; Albumin.] (Physiol. Chem.) Any of a class of toxic substances of protein nature; a toxin.

toxical.c: Toxical Toxic { Tox"ic, Tox"ic*al } (?), a. [L. toxicum poison, originally, a poison in which arrows were dipped, Gr. toxiko`n (sc.?) poison for smearing arrows with, fr. toxiko`s of or for the bow, from to`xon bow, arrow. Cf. Intoxicate.] Of or pertaining to poison; poisonous; as, toxic medicines.

toxicant.c: Toxicant Tox"i*cant (?), n. A poisonous agent or drug, as opium; an intoxicant.

toxication.c: Toxication Tox`i*ca"tion (?), n. [L. toxicum a poison: cf. toxicatus smeared with poison.] Poisoning.

toxicity.c: Toxicity Tox*ic"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being toxic or poisonous; poisonousness.

toxicogenic.c: Toxicogenic Tox`i*co*gen"ic (?), a. [See Toxic, and -genic.] (Physiol. & Med.) Producing toxic products; as, toxicogenic germs or bacteria.

toxicological.c: Toxicological Tox`i*co*log"ic*al (?), a. [Cf.F. toxicologique. ] Of or pertaining to toxicology. -- Tox`i*co*log"ic*al*ly, adv.

toxicologist.c: Toxicologist Tox`i*col"o*gist (?), n. One versed in toxicology; the writer of a treatise on poisons.

toxicology.c: Toxicology Tox`i*col"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. toxiko`n poison + -logy; cf. F. toxicologie. See Toxic. ] The science which treats of poisons, their effects, antidotes, and recognition; also, a discourse or treatise on the science.

toxicomania.c: Toxicomania Tox`i*co*ma"ni*a (?), n. [See. Toxic, and Mania.] 1. (Med.) Toxiphobia. A. S. Taylor.

toxifera.c: Toxifera ‖Tox*if"e*ra (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. to`xon a bow + L. ferre to bear.] (Zool.) Same as Toxoglossa.

toxine.c: Toxine Toxin { Tox"in, Tox"ine } (?), n. [Gr. toxiko`n. See Toxic. ] A poisonous product formed by an organism, such as a pathogenic bacterium, a plant or an animal, usually having a high molecular weight, often a protein or a polysaccharide, but occasionally a low-molecular weight agent such as tetrodotoxin.

toxiphobia.c: Toxiphobia ‖Tox`i*pho"bi*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. toxiko`n poison + fo`bos fear.] (Med.) An insane or greatly exaggerated dread of poisons.

toxodon.c: Toxodon Tox"o*don (?), n. [Gr. to`xon a bow +?,?, a tooth.] (Paleon.) A gigantic extinct herbivorous mammal from South America, having teeth bent like a bow. It is the type of the order Toxodonta.

toxodonta.c: Toxodonta ‖Tox`o*don"ta (?), n.pl. [NL.] (Paleon.) An extinct order of Mammalia found in the South American Tertiary formation. The incisor teeth were long and curved and provided with a persistent pulp. They are supposed to be related both to the rodents and ungulates. Called also Toxodontia.

toxoglossa.c: Toxoglossa ‖Tox`o*glos"sa (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. to`xon a bow +? tongue.] (Zool.) A division of marine gastropod mollusks in which the radula are converted into poison fangs. The cone shells (Conus), Pleurotoma, and Terebra, are examples. See Illust. of Cone, n., 4, Pleurotoma, and Terebra.

toxoid.c: Toxoid Tox"oid (?), n. [Toxin + -oid.] (Physiol. Chem.) An altered form of a toxin, possessing little or no toxic power.

toxophilite.c: Toxophilite Tox*oph"i*lite (?), n. [Gr. to`xon a bow + filei^n to love.] A lover of archery; one devoted to archery.

toxotes.c: Toxotes ‖Tox"o*tes (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? an archer.] (Zool.) A genus of fishes comprising the archer fishes. See Archer fish.

toy.c: Toy Toy (toi), n. [D. tuid tools, implements, stuff, trash, speeltuig playthings, toys; akin to G. zeug stuff, materials, MNG. ziuc, Icel. tygi gear; all ultimately from the root of E. tug, v. t.; cf. G. zeugen to beget, MHG. ziugen to beget, make ready, procure. See Tug, v. t.]
Toy Toy, v. i. [imp. & p. p. toyed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. toying.] To dally amorously; to trifle; to play.
Toy Toy, v. t. To treat foolishly. [Obs.] E. Dering (1576).

toyear.c: Toyear To*year (?), adv. [To, prep. + year. ] This year. [Obs.] Chaucer.

toyer.c: Toyer Toy"er (?), n. One who toys; one who is full of trifling tricks; a trifler.

toyful.c: Toyful Toy"ful (?), a. Full of trifling play. [Obs.] Donne.

toyhouse.c: Toyhouse Toy"house` (?), n. A house for children to play in or to play with; a playhouse.

toyingly.c: Toyingly Toy"ing*ly (?), adv. In a toying manner.

toyman.c: Toyman Toy"man (toi"main), n. One who deals in toys.

toyshop.c: Toyshop Toy"shop` (-shŏp`), n. A shop where toys are sold.

toysome.c: Toysome Toy"some (toi"sŭm), a. Disposed to toy; trifling; wanton. [R.] Ford.

toze.c: Toze Toze (?), v. t. To pull violently; to touse. [Obs.]

tozy.c: Tozy To"zy (?), a. [See Toze ] Soft, like wool that has been teased. -- To"zi*ness (#), n.

trabea.c: Trabea ‖Tra"be*a (?), n.; pl. Trabeae (#). [L.] (Rom. Antiq.) A toga of purple, or ornamented with purple horizontal stripes. -- worn by kings, consuls, and augurs. Dr. W. Smith.

trabeated.c: Trabeated Tra"be*a`ted (?), a. (Arch.) Furnished with an entablature.

trabeation.c: Trabeation Tra`be*a"tion (?), n. [L. trabs, trabis, a beam, a timber.] (Arch.) Same as Entablature.

trabecula.c: Trabecula ‖Tra*bec"u*la (?), n.; pl. Trabeculae (-lē). [L., a little beam.] (Anat.) A small bar, rod, bundle of fibers, or septal membrane, in the framework of an organ part.

trabecular.c: Trabecular Tra*bec"u*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to a trabecula or trabeculae; composed of trabeculae.

trabeculate.c: Trabeculate Tra*bec"u*late (?), a. (Bot.) Crossbarred, as the ducts in a banana stem.

trace.c: Trace Trace (?), n. [F. trais. pl. of trait. See Trait.] 1. One of two straps, chains, or ropes of a harness, extending from the collar or breastplate to a whiffletree attached to a vehicle or thing to be drawn; a tug.

Trace Trace, n. [F. trace. See Trace, v. t. ] 1. A mark left by anything passing; a track; a path; a course; a footprint; a vestige; as, the trace of a carriage or sled; the trace of a deer; a sinuous trace. Milton.

Trace Trace, v. t. [imp. & p. p. traced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. tracing.] [OF. tracier, F. tracer, from (assumed) LL. tractiare, fr.L. tractus, p. p. of trahere to draw. Cf. Abstract, Attract, Contract, Portratt, Tract, Trail, Train, Treat. ] 1. To mark out; to draw or delineate with marks; especially, to copy, as a drawing or engraving, by following the lines and marking them on a sheet superimposed, through which they appear; as, to trace a figure or an outline; a traced drawing.
Trace Trace, v. i. To walk; to go; to travel. [Obs.]

traceable.c: Traceable Trace"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being traced. -- Trace"a*ble*ness, n. -- Trace"a/bly, adv.

tracer.c: Tracer Tra"cer (?), n. One who, or that which, traces.

tracery.c: Tracer/y Tra"cer/y (?), n.; pl. Traceries (?) (Arch.) 1. Ornamental work with rambled lines. Especially: -- (a) The decorative head of a Gothic window.

trachea.c: Trachea Tra"che*a (?), n.; pl. Tracheae (#). [NL.,from L. trachia, Gr. trachei^a (sc.? windpipe), from? rough, rugged: cf. F. trachée.]

tracheal.c: Tracheal Tra"che*al (?), a. [Cf.F. tracheal.] Of or pertaining to the trachea; like a trachea.

trachearia.c: Trachearia ‖Tra`che*a"ri*a (?), n. pl. [NL.] (Zool.) A division of Arachnida including those that breathe only by means of tracheae. It includes the mites, ticks, false scorpions, and harvestmen.

tracheary.c: Tracheary Tra"che*a*ry (?), a. Tracheal; breathing by means of tracheae. -- n. (Zool.) One of the Trachearia.

tracheata.c: Tracheata ‖Tra`che*a"ta (?), n. pl. [NL.] (Zool.) An extensive division of arthropods comprising all those which breathe by tracheae, as distinguished from Crustacea, which breathe by means of branchiae.

tracheate.c: Tracheate Tra"che*ate (?), a. (Zool.) Breathing by means of tracheae; of or pertaining to the Tracheata.
Tracheate Tra"che*ate, n. (Zool.) Any arthropod having tracheae; one of the Tracheata.

tracheid.c: Tracheid Tra"che*id (?), n. (Bot.) A wood cell with spiral or other markings and closed throughout, as in pine wood.

tracheitis.c: Tracheitis ‖Tra`che*i"tis (trā`ke*ī"tĭs), n. [NL. See Trachea; -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the trachea, or windpipe.

trachelidan.c: Trachelidan Tra*chel"i*dan (?), n. [Gr.? neck.] (Zool.) Any one of a tribe of beetles (Trachelides) which have the head supported on a pedicel. The oil beetles and the Cantharides are examples.

trachelipod.c: Trachelipod Tra*chel"i*pod (?), n. [Gr.? neck + -pod:cf.F. trachelipode.] (Zool.) One of the Trachelipoda.

trachelipoda.c: Trachelipoda ‖Tra`che*lip"o*da (?), n. pl. [NL. See Trachelipod.] (Zool.) An extensive artificial group of gastropods comprising all those which have a spiral shell and the foot attached to the base of the neck.

trachelipodous.c: Trachelipodous Tra`che*lip"o*dous (?), a. (Zool.) Having the foot united with the neck; of or pertaining to the Trachelipoda.

trachelobranchiate.c: Trachelobranchiate Tra`che*lo*bran"chi*ate (?), a. [Gr.? + E. tranchiate.] (Zool.) Having the gills situated upon the neck; -- said of certain mollusks.

trachelorrhaphy.c: Trachelorrhaphy Tra`che*lor"rha*phy (?), n. [Gr.? neck +? to sew.] (Med.) The operation of sewing up a laceration of the neck of the uterus.

trachenchyma.c: Trachenchyma ‖Tra*chen"chy*ma (?), n. [NL.,fr. trachea + -enchyma as in E. parenchyma.] (Bot.) A vegetable tissue consisting of tracheae.

tracheobranchia.c: Tracheobranchia ‖Tra`che*o*bran"chi*a (?), n.; pl. Tracheobranchlae (#). [NL. See Trachea, and Branchia.] (Zool.) One of the gill-like breathing organs of certain aquatic insect larvae. They contain tracheal tubes somewhat similar to those of other insects.

tracheobronchial.c: Tracheobronchial Tra`che*o*bron"chi*al (?), a. (Zool.) Pertaining both to the tracheal and bronchial tubes, or to their junction; -- said of the syrinx of certain birds.

tracheocele.c: Tracheocele Tra"che*o*cele (?), n. [Gr.? the windpipe +? a tumor: cf.F. tracheocele. ] (Med.) (a) Goiter. (b) A tumor containing air and communicating with the trachea. Morell Mackenzie.

tracheophonae.c: Tracheophonae ‖Tra`che*oph"o*nae (?), n. pl. [NL., from trachea + Gr. fonei^n to sound.] (Zool.) A group of passerine birds having the syrinx at the lower end of the trachea.

tracheoscopy.c: Tracheoscopy Tra`che*os"co*py (?), n. [Trachea + -scopy.] (Med.) Examination of the interior of the trachea by means of a mirror.

tracheotomy.c: Tracheotomy Tra`che*ot"o*my (?), n. [Trachea + Gr.? to cut: cf.F. tracheotomie.] (Surg.) The operation of making an opening into the windpipe.

trachinoid.c: Trachinoid Tra"chi*noid (?), a. (Zool.) Of, pertaining to, or like, Trachinus, a genus of fishes which includes the weevers. See Weever.

trachoma.c: Trachoma ‖Tra*cho"ma (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? roughness, fr.? rough.] (Med.) a contagious granular conjunctivitis caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis. It is a chronic inflammation of the conjunctiva -- Tra*chom"a*tous (#), a.

trachycarpous.c: Trachycarpous Tra`chy*car"pous (?), a. [Gr.? rough +? fruit.] (Bot.) Rough-fruited. Gray.

trachymedusae.c: Trachymedusae ‖Tra`chy*me*du"sae (?), n. pl. [NL., fr.Gr.? rough + medusa.] (Zool.) A division of acalephs in which the development is direct from the eggs, without a hydroid stage. Some of the species are parasitic on other medusae.

trachyspermous.c: Trachyspermous Tra`chy*sper"mous (?), a. [Gr.? rough +? seed.] (Bot.) Rough-seeded. Gray.

trachystomata.c: Trachystomata ‖Tra`chy*stom"a*ta (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? rough + stoma.] (Zool.) An order of tailed aquatic amphibians, including Siren and Pseudobranchus. They have anterior legs only, are eel-like in form, and have no teeth except a small patch on the palate. The external gills are persistent through life.

trachyte.c: Trachyte Tra"chyte (?), n. [Gr.? rough, rugged: cg. F. trachyte.] (Geol.) An igneous rock, usually light gray in color and breaking with a rough surface. It consists chiefly of orthoclase feldspar with sometimes hornblende and mica.

trachytic.c: Trachytic Tra*chyt"ic (?), a. [Cf. F. trachytique.] Of, pertaining to, or resembling, trachyte.

trachytoid.c: Trachytoid Trach"y*toid (?), a. [Trachyte + -oid.] (Min.) Resembling trachyte; -- used to define the structure of certain rocks.

tracing.c: Tracing Tra"cing (?), n. 1. The act of one who traces; especially, the act of copying by marking on thin paper, or other transparent substance, the lines of a pattern placed beneath; also, the copy thus producted.

track.c: Track Track (?), n. [OF. trac track of horses, mules, trace of animals; of Teutonic origin; cf.D. trek a drawing, trekken to draw, travel, march, MHG. trechen, pret. trach. Cf. Trick.] 1. A mark left by something that has passed along; as, the track, or wake, of a ship; the track of a meteor; the track of a sled or a wheel.

Track Track, v. t. [imp. & p. p. tracked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. tracking.] To follow the tracks or traces of; to pursue by following the marks of the feet; to trace; to trail; as, to track a deer in the snow.

trackage.c: Trackage Track"age (?), n. 1. The act of tracking, or towing, as a boat; towage.

tracker.c: Tracker Track"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, tracks or pursues, as a man or dog that follows game.

tracklayer.c: Tracklayer Track"lay`er (?), n. (Railroads) Any workman engaged in work involved in putting the track in place. [U. S. & Canada] -- Track"lay`ing, n.

trackless.c: Trackless Track"less, a. Having no track; marked by no footsteps; untrodden; as, a trackless desert.

trackman.c: Trackman Track"man (?), n.; pl. -men (?). (Railroads) One employed on work on the track; specif., a trackwalker.

trackmaster.c: Trackmaster Track"mas`ter (?), n. (Railroad) One who has charge of the track; -- called also roadmaster.

trackwalker.c: Trackwalker Track"walk`er (?), n. (Railroads) A person employed to walk over and inspect a section of tracks.

trackway.c: Trackway Track"way` (?), n. Any of two or more narrow paths, of steel, smooth stone, or the like, laid in a public roadway otherwise formed of an inferior pavement, as cobblestones, to provide an easy way for wheels.

tract.c: Tract Tract (?), n. [Abbrev.fr. tractate.] A written discourse or dissertation, generally of short extent; a short treatise, especially on practical religion.

Tract Tract, n. [L. tractus a drawing, train, track, course, tract of land, from trahere tractum, to draw. Senses 4 and 5 are perhaps due to confusion with track. See Trace,v., and cf. Tratt.] 1. Something drawn out or extended; expanse. “The deep tract of hell.” Milton.
Tract Tract, v. t. To trace out; to track; also, to draw out; to protact. [Obs.] Spenser. B. Jonson.

tractability.c: Tractability Tract`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. tractabilitas: cf.F. tractabilite.] The quality or state of being tractable or docile; docility; tractableness.

tractable.c: Tractable Tract"a*ble (?), a. [L. tractabilis, fr, tractare to draw violently, to handle, treat. See Treat, v. t.] 1. Capable of being easily led, taught, or managed; docile; manageable; governable; as, tractable children; a tractable learner.

tractarian.c: Tractarian Trac*ta"ri*an (?), n. (Ch. of England) One of the writers of the Oxford tracts, called “Tracts for the Times,” issued during the period 1833-1841, in which series of papers the sacramental system and authority of the Church, and the value of tradition, were brought into prominence. Also, a member of the High Church party, holding generally the principles of the Tractarian writers; a Puseyite.
Tractarian Trac*ta"ri*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to the Tractarians, or their principles.

tractarianism.c: Tractarianism Trac*ta"ri*an*ism (?), n. (Ch. of England) The principles of the Tractarians, or of those persons accepting the teachings of the “Tracts for the Times.”

tractate.c: Tractate Tract"ate (?), n. [L. tractatus a touching, handling, treatise. See Tractable, and Tract a treatise, Treaty.] A treatise; a tract; an essay.

tractation.c: Tractation Trac*ta"tion (?), n. [L. tractatio.] Treatment or handling of a subject; discussion. [Obs.]

tractator.c: Tractator Trac*ta"tor (?), n. [L., a handler.] One who writes tracts; specif., a Tractarian. [R.] C. Kingsley.

tractile.c: Tractile Tract"ile (?), a. [L. trahere, tractum, to draw.] Capable of being drawn out in length; ductile. Bacon.

tractility.c: Tractility Trac*til"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being tractile; ductility. Derham.

traction.c: Traction Trac"tion (?), n. [L. trahere, tractum, to draw: cf. F. traction.] 1. The act of drawing, or the state of being drawn; as, the traction of a muscle.

Traction wheel Traction wheel. (Mach.) (a) A locomotive driving wheel which acts by friction adhesion to a smooth track. (b) A smooth-rimmed friction wheel for giving motion to an endless link belt or the like.

tractional.c: Tractional Trac"tion*al (?), a. Of or relating to traction.

tractitious.c: Tractitious Trac*ti"tious (?), a. [See Tractate.] Treating of; handling. [R.]

tractive.c: Tractive Tract"ive (?), a. Serving to draw; pulling; attracting; as, tractive power.

tractor.c: Tractor Tract"or (?), n. [NL., from L. trahere, tractum, to draw.] 1. That which draws, or is used for drawing.
Tractor airplane Trac"tor air"plane (?), n. (Aviation) An airplane having one or more tractor propellers; -- called also tractor.

Tractor propeller Tractor screw { Tractor screw or Tractor propeller }. (Aviation) A propeller screw placed in front of the supporting planes of an airplane instead of behind them, so that it exerts a pull instead of a push. Hence, Tractor monoplane, Tractor biplane, etc. This is the most common arrangement for propellers on modern airplanes.

tractory.c: Tractory Tract"o*ry (?), n. [L. tractorius of drawing, fr. trahere, tractum, to draw.] (Geom.) A tractrix.

tractrix.c: Tractrix Tract"rix (?), n. [NL. See Tractor.] (Geom.) A curve such that the part of the tangent between the point of tangency and a given straight line is constant; -- so called because it was conceived as described by the motion of one end of a tangent line as the other end was drawn along the given line.

trad.c: Trad Trad (?), obs. imp. of Tread. Chaucer.

trade.c: Trade Trade (?), n. [Formerly, a path, OE. tred a footmark. See Tread, n. & v.] 1. A track; a trail; a way; a path; also, passage; travel; resort. [Obs.]

Trade Trade (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Traded; p. pr. & vb. n. Trading.] 1. To barter, or to buy and sell; to be engaged in the exchange, purchase, or sale of goods, wares, merchandise, or anything else; to traffic; to bargain; to carry on commerce as a business.
Trade Trade, v. t. To sell or exchange in commerce; to barter.

Trade name Trade name. 1. (a) The name by which an article is called among traders, etc.; as, tin spirits is a common trade name in the dyeing industry for various solutions of tin salts. (b) An invented or arbitrary adopted name given by a manufacturer or merchant to an article to distinguish it as produced or sold by him.

Trade union trades union { trades" un`ion (?), or Trade" un`ion }. An organized combination among workmen for the purpose of maintaining their rights, privileges, and interests with respect to wages, hours of labor, customs, etc.

tradeful.c: Tradeful Trade"ful, a. Full of trade; busy in traffic; commercial. Spenser.

tradeless.c: Tradeless Trade"less, a. Having no trade or traffic. Young.

trademark.c: Trade-mark Trade"-mark` (?), n. A peculiar distinguishing mark or device affixed by a manufacturer or a merchant to his goods, the exclusive right of using which is recognized by law.

trader.c: Trader Trad"er (?), n. 1. One engaged in trade or commerce; one who makes a business of buying and selling or of barter; a merchant; a trafficker; as, a trader to the East Indies; a country trader.

tradescantia.c: Tradescantia ‖Trad`es*can"ti*a (?), prop. n. (Bot.) A genus including spiderwort and Wandering Jew.

tradesfolk.c: Tradesfolk Trades"folk` (?), n. People employed in trade; tradesmen. [R.] Swift.

tradesman.c: Tradesman Trades"man (?), n.; pl. Tradesmen (?). 1. One who trades; a shopkeeper.

tradespeople.c: Tradespeople Trades"peo`ple (?), n. People engaged in trade; shopkeepers.

tradeunionist.c: Trade-unionist Trades-unionist { Trades"-un`ion*ist, Trade"-un`ion*ist }, n. A member of a trades union, or a supporter of trades unions.

tradeswoman.c: Tradeswoman Trades"wom`an (?), n.; pl. Tradeswomen (?). A woman who trades, or is skilled in trade.

trading.c: Trading Trad"ing (?), a. 1. Carrying on trade or commerce; engaged in trade; as, a trading company.

tradition.c: Tradition Tra*di"tion (?), n. [OE. tradicioun, L. traditio, from tradere to give up, transmit. See Treason, Traitor.] 1. The act of delivering into the hands of another; delivery. “A deed takes effect only from the tradition or delivery.” Blackstone.
Tradition Tra*di"tion, v. t. To transmit by way of tradition; to hand down. [Obs.]

traditional.c: Traditional Tra*di"tion*al (?), a. [Cf. F. traditionnel, LL. traditionalis.] 1. Of or pertaining to tradition; derived from tradition; communicated from ancestors to descendants by word only; transmitted from age to age without writing; as, traditional opinions; traditional customs; traditional expositions of the Scriptures.

traditionalism.c: Traditionalism Tra*di"tion*al*ism (?), n. A system of faith founded on tradition; esp., the doctrine that all religious faith is to be based solely upon what is delivered from competent authority, exclusive of rational processes.

traditionalist.c: Traditionalist Tra*di"tion*al*ist (?), n. An advocate of, or believer in, traditionalism; a traditionist.

traditionally.c: Traditionally Tra*di"tion*al*ly, adv. In a traditional manner.

traditionary.c: Traditionary Tra*di"tion*a*ry, n.; pl. Traditionaries (?). [Cf. F. traditionnare.] One, among the Jews, who acknowledges the authority of traditions, and explains the Scriptures by them.

traditionist.c: Traditionist Traditioner { Tra*di"tion*er (?), Tra*di"tion*ist, } n. [Cf. F. traditionniste.] One who adheres to tradition.

traditive.c: Traditive Trad"i*tive (?), a. [L. tradere, traditum, to transmit, give up: cf. F. traditif.] Transmitted or transmissible from father to son, or from age, by oral communication; traditional. [R.] Jer. Taylor.

traditor.c: Traditor ‖Trad"i*tor (?), n. [L., fr. tradere, traditum. See Traitor.] (Eccl. Hist.) A deliverer; -- a name of infamy given to Christians who delivered the Scriptures, or the goods of the church, to their persecutors to save their lives. Milner.

traduce.c: Traduce Tra*duce" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Traduced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Traducing (?).] [L. traducere, traductum, to lead across, lead along, exhibit as a spectacle, disgrace, transfer, derive; trans across, over + ducere to lead: cf. F. traduire to transfer, translate, arraign, fr. L. traducere. See Duke.] 1. To transfer; to transmit; to hand down; as, to traduce mental qualities to one's descendants. [Obs.] Glanvill.

traducement.c: Traducement Tra*duce"ment (?), n. The act of traducing; misrepresentation; ill-founded censure; defamation; calumny. [R.] Shak.

traducent.c: Traducent Tra*du"cent (?), a. [L. traducens, p. pr. of traducere. See Traduce.] Slanderous. [R.] Entick.

traducer.c: Traducer Tra*du"cer (?), n. 1. One who traduces; a slanderer; a calumniator. Bp. Hall.

traducian.c: Traducian Tra*du"cian (?), n. A believer in traducianism.

traducianism.c: Traducianism Tra*du"cian*ism (?), n. (Theol.) The doctrine that human souls are produced by the act of generation; -- opposed to creationism, and infusionism.

traducible.c: Traducible Tra*du"ci*ble, a. 1. Capable of being derived or propagated. [Obs.] Sir M. Hale.

traducingly.c: Traducingly Tra*du"cing*ly, adv. In a traducing manner; by traduction; slanderously.

traduct.c: Traduct Tra*duct" (?), v. t. [L. traducere, traductum. See Traduce.] To derive or deduce; also, to transmit; to transfer. [Obs.] Fotherby.
Traduct Tra*duct", n. That which is traducted; that which is transferred; a translation. [Obs.] Howell.

traduction.c: Traduction Tra*duc"tion (?), n. [L. traductio a transferring: cf. F. traduction translation. See Traduce.] 1. Transmission from one to another. [Obs.]

traductive.c: Traductive Tra*duc"tive (?), a. Capable of being deduced; derivable. [R.] Bp. Warburton.

traffic.c: Traffic Traf"fic (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Trafficked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Trafficking (?).] [F. trafiquer; cf. It. trafficare, Sp. traficar, trafagar, Pg. traficar, trafegar, trafeguear, LL. traficare; of uncertain origin, perhaps fr. L. trans across, over + -ficare to make (see -fy, and cf. G. übermachen to transmit, send over, e. g., money, wares); or cf. Pg. trasfegar to pour out from one vessel into another, OPg. also, to traffic, perhaps fr. (assumed) LL. vicare to exchange, from L. vicis change (cf. Vicar).] 1. To pass goods and commodities from one person to another for an equivalent in goods or money; to buy or sell goods; to barter; to trade.
Traffic Traf"fic, v. t. To exchange in traffic; to effect by a bargain or for a consideration.

Traffic Traf"fic, n. [Cf. F. trafic, It. traffico, Sp. tráfico, tráfago, Pg. tráfego, LL. traficum, trafica. See Traffic, v.] 1. Commerce, either by barter or by buying and selling; interchange of goods and commodities; trade.

Traffic mile Traf"fic mile. (Railroad Accounting) Any unit of the total obtained by adding the passenger miles and ton miles in a railroad's transportation for a given period; -- a term and practice of restricted or erroneous usage.

trafficable.c: Trafficable Traf"fic*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being disposed of in traffic; marketable. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

trafficker.c: Trafficker Traf"fick*er (?), n. One who traffics, or carries on commerce; a trader; a merchant.

trafficless.c: Trafficless Traf"fic*less, a. Destitute of traffic, or trade.

tragacanth.c: Tragacanth Trag"a*canth (?), n. [L. tragacanthum tragacanth, tragacantha the plant producing tragacanth, Gr.?? a he-goat +? a thorn: cf. F. tragacanthe.] A kind of gum procured from a spiny leguminous shrub (Astragalus gummifer) of Western Asia, and other species of Astragalus. It comes in hard whitish or yellowish flakes or filaments, and is nearly insoluble in water, but slowly swells into a mucilaginous mass, which is used as a substitute for gum arabic in medicine and the arts. Called also gum tragacanth.

tragedienne.c: Tragedienne ‖Tra`gé`dienne" (trȧ`zha`dyĕn"; Eng. trȧ*jē"dĭ*ĕn`), n. [F.] A woman who plays in tragedy.

tragedious.c: Tragedious Tra*ge"di*ous (?), a. Like tragedy; tragical. [Obs.] “Tragedious history.” Fabyan.

tragedy.c: Tragedy Trag"e*dy (?), n.; pl. Tragedies (#). [OE. tragedie, OF. tragedie, F. tragédie, L. tragoedia, Gr.?, fr.? a tragic poet and singer, originally, a goat singer;? a goat (perhaps akin to? to gnaw, nibble, eat, and E. trout) +? to sing; from the oldest tragedies being exhibited when a goat was sacrificed, or because a goat was the prize, or because the actors were clothed in goatskins. See Ode.]

tragical.c: Tragical Tragic { Trag"ic (?), Trag"ic*al (?), } a. [L. tragicus, Gr.?: cf. F. tragique.] 1. Of or pertaining to tragedy; of the nature or character of tragedy; as, a tragic poem; a tragic play or representation.

tragic.c: Tragic Trag"ic (?), n. 1. A writer of tragedy. [Obs.]

tragicomedy.c: Tragi-comedy Trag`i-com"e*dy (?), n. [Cf. F. tragicomédie, L. tragicocomoedia. See Tragic, and Comedy.] A kind of drama representing some action in which serious and comic scenes are blended; a composition partaking of the nature both of tragedy and comedy.

tragicomical.c: Tragi-comical Tragi-comic { Trag`i-com"ic (?), Trag`i-com"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. tragi-comique.] Of or pertaining to tragi-comedy; partaking of grave and comic scenes. -- Trag`-com"ic*al*ly, adv.

tragicomipastoral.c: Tragi-comi-pastoral Trag`i-com`i-pas"tor*al (?), a. Partaking of the nature of, or combining, tragedy, comedy, and pastoral poetry. [R.] Gay.

tragopan.c: Tragopan Trag"o*pan (?), n. [NL., fr. L. tragopan a fabulous Ethiopian bird, Gr.?.] (Zool.) Any one of several species of Asiatic pheasants of the genus Ceriornis. They are brilliantly colored with a variety of tints, the back and breast are usually covered with white or buff ocelli, and the head is ornamented with two bright-colored, fleshy wattles. The crimson tragopan, or horned pheasant (Ceriornis satyra), of India is one of the best-known species.

tragus.c: Tragus ‖Tra"gus (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a part of the inner ear.] (Anat.) The prominence in front of the external opening of the ear. See Illust. under Ear.

trail.c: Trail Trail (trāl), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Trailed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Trailing.] [OE. trailen, OF. trailler to trail a deer, or hunt him upon a cold scent, also, to hunt or pursue him with a limehound, F. trailler to trail a fishing line; probably from a derivative of L. trahere to draw; cf. L. traha a drag, sledge, tragula a kind of drag net, a small sledge, Sp. trailla a leash, an instrument for leveling the ground, D. treilen to draw with a rope, to tow, treil a rope for drawing a boat. See Trace, v. t.]
Trail Trail (?), v. i. 1. To be drawn out in length; to follow after.
Trail Trail, n. 1. A track left by man or beast; a track followed by the hunter; a scent on the ground by the animal pursued; as, a deer trail.
Trail rope Trail rope. (Aeronautics) Same as Guide rope, above.

trailer.c: Trailer Trail"er (?), n. One who, or that which, trails.

trailing.c: Trailing Trail"ing, a. & vb. n. from Trail.
Trailing edge Trail"ing edge. (Aeronautics) A following edge. See Advancing edge, above.

train.c: Train Train (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Trained (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Training.] [OF. trahiner, traïner,F. traîner, LL. trahinare, trainare, fr. L. trahere to draw. See Trail.]
Train Train, v. i. 1. To be drilled in military exercises; to do duty in a military company.

Train Train, n. [F. train, OF. traïn, trahin; cf. (for some of the senses) F. traine. See Train, v.] 1. That which draws along; especially, persuasion, artifice, or enticement; allurement. [Obs.] “Now to my charms, and to my wily trains.” Milton.
Train dispatcher Train dispatcher. An official who gives the orders on a railroad as to the running of trains and their right of way.
Train oil Train" oil` (oil`). [D. or LG. traan train oil, blubber (cf. Dan. & Sw. tran, G. thran) + E. oil.] Oil procured from the blubber or fat of whales, by boiling.

trainable.c: Trainable Train"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being trained or educated; as, boys trainable to virtue. Richardson.

trainband.c: Trainband Train"band` (?), n.; pl. Trainbands (?). A band or company of an organized military force instituted by James I. and dissolved by Charles II.; -- afterwards applied to the London militia. [Eng.]

trainbearer.c: Trainbearer Train"bear`er (?), n. One who holds up a train, as of a robe.

trainer.c: Trainer Train"er (?), n. 1. One who trains; an instructor; especially, one who trains or prepares men, horses, etc., for exercises requiring physical agility and strength.

training.c: Training Train"ing, n. The act of one who trains; the act or process of exercising, disciplining, etc.; education.

trainy.c: Trainy Train"y (?), a. Belonging to train oil. [Obs.] Gay.

traipse.c: Traipse Traipse (?), v. i. [Cf. G. trapsen, trappsen, trappen, to tread noisily, to walk stamping. See Trample, Trape.] To walk or run about in a slatternly, careless, or thoughtless manner. [Colloq.] Pope.

trays.c: Trays Trais { Trais (?), Trays }, n. pl. Traces. [Obs.]
Trays Trays (?), n. pl. [Obs.] See Trais. Chaucer.

trait.c: Trait Trait (?), n. [F., fr. L. tractus, fr. trahere to draw. See Trace, v., and cf. Tract a region, Trace a strap, Tret.]

traiteur.c: Traiteur ‖Trai`teur" (?), n. [F.] The keeper of an eating house, or restaurant; a restaurateur. Simmonds.

traitor.c: Traitor Trai"tor (?), n. [OE. traitour, OF. traïtor, traïteur, F. treître, L. traditor, fr. tradere, traditum, to deliver, to give up or surrender treacherously, to betray; trans across, over + dare to give. See Date time, and cf. Betray,Tradition, Traditor, Treason.] 1. One who violates his allegiance and betrays his country; one guilty of treason; one who, in breach of trust, delivers his country to an enemy, or yields up any fort or place intrusted to his defense, or surrenders an army or body of troops to the enemy, unless when vanquished; also, one who takes arms and levies war against his country; or one who aids an enemy in conquering his country. See Treason.
Traitor Trai"tor, v. t. To act the traitor toward; to betray; to deceive. [Obs.] “ But time, it traitors me.” Lithgow.

traitoress.c: Traitoress Trai"tor*ess (?), n. A traitress. [Obs.] Rom. of R.

traitorly.c: Traitorly Trai"tor*ly (?), a. Like a traitor; treacherous; traitorous. [Obs.] “Traitorly rascals.” Shak.

traitorous.c: Traitorous Trai"tor*ous (?), a. [Cf. F. traîtreux.] 1. Guilty of treason; treacherous; perfidious; faithless; as, a traitorous officer or subject. Shak.

traitress.c: Traitress Trai"tress (?), n. [F. traîtresse.] A woman who betrays her country or any trust; a traitoress. Dryden.

traject.c: Traject Tra*ject" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Trajected; p. pr. & vb. n. Trajecting.] [L. trajectus, p. p. of trajicere to throw across; trans across + jacere to throw. See Jet a shooting forth.] To throw or cast through, over, or across; as, to traject the sun's light through three or more cross prisms. [R.] Sir I. Newton.
Traject Traj"ect (?), n. [L. trajectus, fr. trajicere: cf. F. trajet, OF. traject. See Traject, v. t.] 1. A place for passing across; a passage; a ferry. [Obs.] Cotgrave.

trajection.c: Trajection Tra*jec"tion (?), n. [L. trajectio a crossing over, transposition.] 1. The act of trajecting; a throwing or casting through or across; also, emission. Boyle.

trajectory.c: Trajectory Tra*ject"o*ry (?), n.; pl. Trajectories (#). [Cf. F. trajectoire.] The curve which a body describes in space, as a planet or comet in its orbit, or stone thrown upward obliquely in the air.

trajetry.c: Trajetry Trajetour Trajet { Tra"jet (?), Tra"jet*our (?), Tra"jet*ry (?) }, n. See Treget, Tregetour, and Tregetry. [Obs.]

tralation.c: Tralation Tra*la"tion (?), n. [L. tralatio, translatio.See Translation.] The use of a word in a figurative or extended sense; ametaphor; a trope. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

tralatition.c: Tralatition Tral`a*ti"tion (?), n. [See Tralatitious.] A change, as in the use of words; a metaphor.

tralatitious.c: Tralatitious Tral`a*ti"tious (?), a. [L. tralatitius, translatitius, tralaticius, translaticius. See Tralation.] 1. Passed along; handed down; transmitted.

tralatitiously.c: Tralatitiously Tral`a*ti"tious*ly, adv. In a tralatitious manner; metephorically. Holder.

tralineate.c: Tralineate Tra*lin"e*ate (?), v. i. [L. trans across + linea a line: cf. It tralineare, tralignare.] To deviate; to stray; to wander. [Obs.] Dryden.

tralucency.c: Tralucency Tra*lu"cen*cy (?), n. Translucency; as, the tralucency of a gem. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

tralucent.c: Tralucent Tra*lu"cent (?), a. [L. tralucens, translucens, p. pr. See Translucent.] Translucent. [Obs.]

tram.c: Tram Tram (?), n. [Prov. E. tram a coal wagon, the shaft of a cart or carriage, a beam or bar; probably of Scand, origin; cf. OSw. tråm, trum, a beam, OD. drom, Prov. & OHG. tram.] 1. A four-wheeled truck running on rails, and used in a mine, as for carrying coal or ore.

Tram Tram, n. [Sp. trama weft, or F. trame.] A silk thread formed of two or more threads twisted together, used especially for the weft, or cross threads, of the best quality of velvets and silk goods.
Tram Tram, n. (Mech.) Same as Trammel, n., 6.
Tram Tram (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Trammed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Tramming.] To convey or transport on a tramway or on a tram car.
Tram Tram, v. i. To operate, or conduct the business of, a tramway; to travel by tramway.

trama.c: Trama ‖Tra"ma (?), n. [L., woof.] (Bot.) The loosely woven substance which lines the chambers within the gleba in certain Gasteromycetes.

tramble.c: Tramble Tram"ble (?), v. t. (Mining) To wash, as tin ore, with a shovel in a frame fitted for the purpose. Smart.

trammel.c: Trammel Tram"mel (?), n. [F. tramail, trémail, a net, LL. tremaculum, tremacle, a kind of net for taking fish; L. tres three + macula a mesh. See Three, and Mail armor.] 1. A kind of net for catching birds, fishes, or other prey. Carew.
Trammel Tram"mel (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Trammeled (?) or Trammelled; p. pr. & vb. n. Trammeling, or Trammelling.] 1. To entangle, as in a net; to catch. [R.] Shak.

Trammel wheel Tram"mel wheel`. (Mach.) A circular plate or a cross, with two or more cross grooves intersecting at the center, used on the end of a shaft to transmit motion to another shaft not in line with the first.

trammeled.c: Trammeled Tram"meled (?), a. (Man.) Having blazes, or white marks, on the fore and hind foot of one side, as if marked by trammels; -- said of a horse. [Written also trammelled.]

trammeler.c: Trammeler Tram"mel*er (?), n. [Written also trammeller.] 1. One who uses a trammel net. Nares.

tramming.c: Tramming Tram"ming (?), n. (Silk Manuf.) The act or process of forming trams. See 2d Tram.

tramontana.c: Tramontana ‖Tra`mon*ta"na (?), n. [It. See Tramontane.] (Meteor.) A dry, cold, violent, northerly wind of the Adriatic.

tramontane.c: Tramontane Tra*mon"tane (?), a. [OF. tramontain, It. tramontano, L. transmontanus; trans across, beyond + mons, montis, mountain.] Lying or being beyond the mountains; coming from the other side of the mountains; hence, foreign; barbarous.
Tramontane Tra*mon"tane, n. One living beyond the mountains; hence, a foreigner; a stranger.

tramp.c: Tramp Tramp (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Tramped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Tramping.] [OE. trampen; akin to LG. trampen, G. trampeln, LG. & D. trappen, Dan. trampe, Sw. & Icel. trampa, Goth. anatrimpan to press upon; also to D. trap a step, G. treppe steps, stairs. Cf. Trap a kind of rock, Trape, Trip, v. i., Tread.] 1. To tread upon forcibly and repeatedly; to trample.
Tramp Tramp, v. i. To travel; to wander; to stroll.
Tramp Tramp, n. 1. A foot journey or excursion; as, to go on a tramp; a long tramp. Blackie.

tramper.c: Tramper Tramp"er (?), n. One who tramps; a stroller; a vagrant or vagabond; a tramp. Dickens.

trample.c: Trample Tram"ple (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Trampled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Trampling (?).] [OE. trampelen, freq. of trampen. See Tramp, v. t.] 1. To tread under foot; to tread down; to prostrate by treading; as, to trample grass or flowers. Dryden.
Trample Tram"ple, v. i. 1. To tread with force and rapidity; to stamp.
Trample Tram"ple, n. The act of treading under foot; also, the sound produced by trampling. Milton.

trampler.c: Trampler Tram"pler (?), n. One who tramples; one who treads down; as, a trampler on nature's law. Cowper.

trampoose.c: Trampoose Tram*poose" (?), v. i. [See Tramp, Trample, and Traipse.] To walk with labor, or heavily; to tramp. [Law, U. S.] Bartlett.

tramrail.c: Tramrail Tram"rail` (?), n. (Mach.) An overhead rail forming a track on which a trolley runs to convey a load, as in a shop.

tramroad.c: Tramroad Tram"road` (?), n. [Tram a coal wagon + road.] A road prepared for easy transit of trams or wagons, by forming the wheel tracks of smooth beams of wood, blocks of stone, or plates of iron.

tranation.c: Tranation Tra*na"tion (?), n. [L. tranare, transnare, to swim over; trans across, over + nare to swim.] The act of swimming over. [Obs.] Bailey.

trance.c: Trance Trance (?), n. [F. transe fright, in OF. also, trance or swoon, fr. transir to chill, benumb, to be chilled, to shiver, OF. also, to die, L. transire to pass over, go over, pass away, cease; trans across, over + ire to go; cf. L. transitus a passing over. See Issue, and cf. Transit.]
Trance Trance, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Tranced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Trancing (?).] 1. To entrance.
Trance Trance (?), v. i. To pass; to travel. [Obs.]

tranect.c: Tranect Tran"ect (?), n. [Cf. Traject.] A ferry. [Obs.] Shak.

trangram.c: Trangram Tran"gram (?), n. [OE. trangrain a strange thing, trangame a toy. See Tangram.] Something intricately contrived; a contrived; a puzzle. [Cant & Obs.] Arbuthnot.

tranquil.c: Tranquil Tran"quil (?), a. [L. tranquillus; probably fr. trans across, over + a word akin to quietus quiet: cf. F. tranquille. See Quiet.] Quiet; calm; undisturbed; peaceful; not agitated; as, the atmosphere is tranquil; the condition of the country is tranquil.

tranquillization.c: Tranquillization Tranquilization { Tran`quil*i*za"tion, Tran`quil*li*za"tion } (?), n. The act of tranquilizing, or the state of being tranquilized.

tranquillize.c: Tranquillize Tranquilize {Tran"quil*ize, Tran"quil*lize } (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Tranquilized (?) or Tranquilliized; p. pr. & vb. n. Tranquilizing (?) or Tranquillizing.] [Cf. F. tranquilliser.] To render tranquil; to allay when agitated; to compose; to make calm and peaceful; as, to tranquilize a state disturbed by factions or civil commotions; to tranquilize the mind.

tranquillizer.c: Tranquillizer Tranquilizer { Tran"quil*i`zer, Tran"quil*li`zer } (?), n. One who, or that which, tranquilizes.

tranquillizing.c: Tranquillizing Tranquilizing { Tran"quil*i`zing, Tran"quil*li`zing } (?), a. Making tranquil; calming. “ The tranquilizing power of time.” Wordsworth. -- Tran"quil*i`zing*ly or Tran"quil*li`zing*ly, adv.

tranquillity.c: Tranquillity Tran*quil"li*ty (?), n. [F. tranquillité, L. tranquillitas.] The quality or state of being tranquil; calmness; composure.

tranquilly.c: Tranquilly Tran"quil*ly (?), adv. In a tranquil manner; calmly.

tranquilness.c: Tranquilness Tran"quil*ness, n. Quality or state of being tranquil.

trans.c: Trans- Trans- (?). [L. trans across, over.] A prefix, signifying over, beyond, through and through, on the other side, as in transalpine, beyond the Alps; transform, to form through and through, that is, anew, transfigure.

transact.c: Transact Trans*act" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Transacted; p. pr. & vb. n. Transacting.] [L. transactus, p. p. of transigere. See Transaction.] To carry through; to do; perform; to manage; as, to transact commercial business; to transact business by an agent.
Transact Trans*act", v. i. To conduct matters; to manage affairs. [R.] South.

transaction.c: Transaction Trans*ac"tion (?), n. [L. transactio, fr. transigere, transactum, to drive through, carry through, accomplish, transact; trans across, over + agere to drive; cf. F. transaction. See Act, Agent.] 1. The doing or performing of any business; management of any affair; performance.

transactor.c: Transactor Trans*act"or (?), n. [L.] One who transacts, performs, or conducts any business. Derham.

transalpine.c: Transalpine Trans*al"pine (?), a. [L. transalpinus; trans across, beyond + Alpinus Alpine, from Alpes the Alps: cf. F. transalpin.] Being on the farther side of the Alps in regard to Rome, that is, on the north or west side of the Alps; of or pertaining to the region or the people beyond the Alps; as, transalpine Gaul; -- opposed to cisalpine. “ Transalpine garbs.” Beau. & Fl.
Transalpine Trans*al"pine, n. A native or inhabitant of a country beyond the Alps, that is, out of Italy.

transanimate.c: Transanimate Trans*an"i*mate (trăns*ăn"ĭ*māt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Transanimated (trăns*ăn"ĭ*mā`tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Transanimating.] [Trans- + animate.] To animate with a soul conveyed from another body. [R.] Bp. J. King (1608).

transanimation.c: Transanimation Trans*an`i*ma"tion (trăns*ăn`ĭ*mā"shŭn), n. [Cf. F. transanimation.] The conveyance of a soul from one body to another. [R.] Fuller.

transatlantic.c: Transatlantic Trans`at*lan"tic (trăns*ăt*lăn"tĭk), a. [Pref. trans- + Atlantic: cf. F. transatlantique.] 1. Lying or being beyond the Atlantic Ocean.

transaudient.c: Transaudient Trans*au"di*ent (trăns*ä"dĭ*eint), a. [See Trans-, and Audient.] Permitting the passage of sound. [R.] Lowell.

transcalency.c: Transcalency Trans*ca"len*cy (trăns*kā"lein*sy̆), n. The quality or state of being transcalent.

transcalent.c: Transcalent Trans*ca"lent (trăns*kā"leint), a. [Pref. trans- + L. calens, p. pr. of calere to grow warm.] Pervious to, or permitting the passage of, heat.

transcend.c: Transcend Tran*scend" (trăn*sĕnd"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Transcended; p. pr. & vb. n. Transcending.] [L. transcendere, transcensum; trans beyond, over + scandere to climb. See Scan.] 1. To rise above; to surmount; as, lights in the heavens transcending the region of the clouds. Howell.
Transcend Tran*scend" (trăn*sĕnd"), v. i. 1. To climb; to mount. [Obs.]

transcendency.c: Transcendency Transcendence { Tran*scend"ence (-eins), Tran*scend"en*cy (-ein*sy̆), }[Cf. L. transcendentia, F. transcendance.] 1. The quality or state of being transcendent; superior excellence; supereminence.

transcendent.c: Transcendent Tran*scend"ent (?), a. [L. transcendens, -entis, p. pr. of transcendere to transcend: cf. F. transcendant, G. transcendent.] 1. Very excellent; superior or supreme in excellence; surpassing others; as, transcendent worth; transcendent valor.
Transcendent Tran*scend"ent, n. That which surpasses or is supereminent; that which is very excellent.
